subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 6 periods = 240 minutes
Total: 6 periods · 4h 0min

periods.activity_title: Who Is in Bela's Family? Who Is in Mine?
periods.textbook_anchor: Singing Together — Write the names of your family members in the table (p. 6)
materials: Notebook or loose sheet for each student

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads aloud the opening of the chapter, introducing Bela, Banku Bhaiya, little Bishu, and the flowering garden where the family gathers. Students listen and then share: who lives in their own home? A quick show of hands reveals the range of family sizes in the class — some have grandparents at home, some do not, and both are welcomed.

Whole-class discussion: What do Bela and her family enjoy doing together outdoors? Students connect this to their own experience — games they play at home, people they play with, and what makes those times special. The teacher draws out that families spend time together in different ways in different homes, and that all of those ways count.

Students open Textbook p. 6 and write the names of their family members in the table. The teacher circulates, asking each child to say aloud one name and their relation — 'This is Nani, my mother's mother.' Students who have small families and students with large joint families are each invited to share, so the class sees the variety.

Pair share: each student tells their partner one thing their family loves to do together — a game, an evening routine, a song. Two or three pairs share with the class. The teacher closes by naming what the class discovered: families come in many shapes and sizes, and all are held together by the time people spend with each other.

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe the members and shared activities of a family, connecting a textbook account to their own lived experience.
periods.section_context: Bela's family — Banku Bhaiya, Bishu, parents, Dadiji, Dadaji; chhupan-chhupai, peek-a-boo; flowering garden as gathering space; family members table on p. 6.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Does every family do the same things together?' — let children notice difference without hierarchy. If a child names a neighbour or a relative who visits often as 'family', welcome it; the chapter itself broadens that boundary.

periods.textbook_anchor: Singing Together — Think of a rain song and sing it with your friends in the class (p. 6)

time_bands.activity: The teacher sets the scene: it is a rainy day, the family is inside the garden shelter, and Dadiji is singing. Students are asked: what does your family do when it rains heavily and everyone stays indoors? A few children share — board games, stories, cooking together, watching rain. The teacher notes that Bela's family plays antakshari and snakes and ladders.

Students open Textbook p. 6 and read the rain song together. The teacher reads it once expressively, then the class reads it aloud together. The teacher asks: has anyone heard a song about rain at home — from a grandparent, a parent, or at a local festival? Students share any rain songs, rhymes, or chants they know, in any language. Each song is welcomed and briefly sung or spoken aloud by the child who brought it.

Students choose one rain song they know — the textbook song or one from home — and write it in their notebook, decorating the border with a quick drawing of rain, clouds, or whatever the song makes them think of. Children who cannot recall a rain song may write two lines about what they love to do on rainy days. The teacher circulates and asks children to hum their song softly as they write.

Three or four volunteers sing or recite their song or lines to the class. The teacher reflects aloud: Dadiji learned her rain song from someone older than her, and now Bela knows it — songs travel from person to person across many years. The class has just done the same thing.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify and share a folk or traditional song from their own environment, recognising oral transmission as a way knowledge passes between generations.
periods.section_context: Rainy-day shelter gathering; antakshari, snakes and ladders; Dadiji's traditional rain songs; oral transmission across generations; rain song on p. 6.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt: 'Did someone teach you that song, or did you learn it yourself?' — this surfaces the idea of learning from elders without naming it as a formal concept. Accept songs in any regional language; the diversity of songs across the class is itself the learning.

periods.activity_title: Games Across Generations — Grandparents' Play and Ours
periods.textbook_anchor: Laughing Together — Do you know what games your grandparents used to play when they were young? (p. 7)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens with Textbook p. 7: Dadaji joins the children in their games and plays alongside them. Ask students: have you ever played a game with a grandparent, an older relative, or an elderly neighbour? What was that like? A few students share briefly. The teacher notes that the chapter asks a question many of them may need to investigate — what games did grandparents play as children?

Class discussion: students share whatever they already know about games their grandparents or older relatives have mentioned — gilli-danda, kabaddi, lattu, marbles, langdi, and others come up naturally. The teacher writes game names on the board as they are mentioned, making a growing list. Students also discuss which of these games they themselves have played and which are new to them.

Students open Textbook p. 8 and discuss in pairs: what games do you play with elders and other family members at home? Each pair writes three games in their notebook — one they play with grandparents or elders, one they play with parents or siblings, and one they play with friends their own age. The teacher draws attention to the family pet and neighbourhood animals mentioned in the section, asking which animals come to their home or neighbourhood (Textbook p. 8).

Pairs share their lists. The teacher builds a simple two-column display on the board: 'Games from long ago' and 'Games we play now.' The class looks at the overlap — pitthoo, chhupan-chhupai, and antakshari appear in both columns for many children. The teacher reflects: when Dadaji plays with the children, old games and new ones meet in the same afternoon.

periods.implied_lo: Students can compare games played across different generations, identifying continuity and change in family and community play traditions.
periods.section_context: Dadaji playing traditional games with children; chhupan-chhupai, peek-a-boo, gilli-danda, kabaddi, lattu; family pet dog Shiru; neighbourhood animals — cows, buffaloes, dogs, parrots, cats, goats; games across generations discussion.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Why do you think Dadaji still enjoys playing with you?' — this opens a conversation about intergenerational care without being didactic. Children who do not have grandparents at home can think of any older person they know; the question is about connection, not household structure.

periods.activity_title: Rangoli from the Garden — A Community Craft
periods.textbook_anchor: Helping Each Other — Collect some leaves and flowers that have fallen on the ground and create a rangoli (p. 12)
materials: Fallen leaves and flowers collected from the school compound
A sheet of paper or open floor space per group
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustration of Munni making rangoli with natural materials

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads the section passage about Kusum Mausi cooking festival sweets and Munni making rangoli using colours from dried flowers and leaves. Students open Textbook p. 12 and look at the illustration. Ask: have you seen rangoli at home or in your neighbourhood? Who makes it, and when? Students share briefly — festivals, special guests, daily doorstep patterns in some communities.

In small groups students step outside to the school compound and collect fallen leaves, flowers, petals, seeds, or bark — only what has already fallen, not plucked. The teacher reminds them: Munni's rangoli used materials from the ground around her; so will ours. Groups return to the classroom with their collected material.

Each group arranges their natural materials into a rangoli pattern on their sheet of paper or a section of floor. No glue is needed — the arrangement itself is the design. The teacher circulates, asking each group what shape or pattern they chose and why, and inviting children to name the materials they used. Groups whose schools have limited fallen material may supplement with safe classroom materials such as chalk lines or cut paper, arranged in the same spirit.

Groups briefly present their rangoli to the class — what materials they used, what pattern they made. The teacher draws the connection to Textbook p. 12: Munni's tradition came from her community and uses what the earth offers. The class has done something similar today. Students note in their notebooks: three materials they used and one word describing their pattern.

periods.implied_lo: Students can create a simple design using locally gathered natural materials, connecting the activity to a community craft tradition described in the chapter.
periods.section_context: Munni's rangoli using dried flowers and leaves; Kusum Mausi's festival sweets; community as extension of family; fallen leaves, flowers, petals, seeds as craft materials; rangoli activity on p. 12.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Where did Munni learn to make rangoli?' — let children arrive at the answer that it came from watching and helping within the community. This surfaces the idea of learning through participation rather than instruction, without labelling it.

periods.activity_title: Who Does What at Home — Mapping Family Work
periods.textbook_anchor: Helping Each Other — Who does what work in your family? Find out and fill in the table (p. 15)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustrations showing family members doing household tasks (p. 9)

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 9 and look at the activity showing different household tasks — cooking, gardening, cleaning, caring for others. Students tick and colour the activities they recognise from their own homes. The teacher circulates and notices which tasks appear most and least often, ready to reflect this back to the class.

Students turn to Textbook p. 15 and look at the table structure for recording who does what work in the family. The teacher reads aloud the task: find out and fill in the table. Since this requires knowledge from home, students work from memory now and are invited to add or correct entries after they next speak with family members. Each student fills in the table with what they already know — who cooks, who cleans, who helps with homework, who cares for grandparents or younger children.

Pairs compare their tables: are the same tasks shared the same way in both families? Students discuss what they notice — some tasks are shared by many people, some are done by one person, and in some families children themselves help with specific tasks. The teacher draws attention to the chapter's examples: Banku chops vegetables, Bela helps Dadaji in the garden, parents share cooking and cleaning.

Brief whole-class reflection: students share one task they themselves do at home. The teacher records responses on the board and the class sees that children contribute meaningfully to family life — not as a chore, but as a form of care. Students write one sentence in their notebook: 'One way I help my family is …'

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe and record how household work is shared among family members, noticing patterns of contribution and care.
periods.section_context: Dadiji oiling and braiding Bela's hair; parents sharing cooking and cleaning; Banku chopping vegetables; Bela helping Dadaji in the garden; household task illustrations on p. 9; family work table on p. 15; relatives visiting — relatives table on p. 15.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Does anyone in this room do something at home that surprised their family when they started doing it?' — this invites children to see their own contribution as meaningful. Avoid framing any task as belonging to one gender or age; the chapter models shared work deliberately.

periods.activity_title: Pitthoo in the Park — Drawing Happy Moments Together
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Draw some of the happy moments you enjoy together with your family (p. 17)
materials: Drawing sheet or open notebook page
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustration of the pitthoo game in the park

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads the closing section of the chapter: Bela's family goes to the park, joins friends playing pitthoo — stacked stones, a ball, two teams — and Dadaji plays actively alongside the children. Students discuss: have you played pitthoo, or a game like it? What makes a game fun when people of different ages play together? Two or three students share.

Students open Textbook p. 17 and read the two Let us reflect prompts about family love and games they play with friends. A brief pair discussion: how do the people in your family show they care for each other — through play, food, help, stories, or something else? Students share one example each.

Students turn to Textbook p. 17 and begin the drawing task: draw some of the happy moments you enjoy with your family. Each student draws one clear scene — a game, a meal, a song, a garden moment, or anything that captures togetherness in their family. Below the drawing they write two sentences describing what is happening and who is there. The teacher circulates, asking each child to describe their scene aloud as they draw, helping them find words for what they are making.

A gallery walk: drawings are placed on desks and students move around quietly to look at three classmates' work, then return to their seat. The teacher closes: every drawing in this room shows a different family — different faces, different games, different foods — and every one of them is full of care. That is what this chapter is about.

periods.implied_lo: Students can represent a personal experience of family togetherness through drawing and writing, connecting it to the chapter's themes of shared play and intergenerational care.
periods.section_context: Pitthoo game — stacked stones, ball, two teams; park outing with Dadaji; ice cream and laughter; Let us reflect drawing task on p. 17; happy family moments; intergenerational play.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'What would you want someone who has never met your family to know about them, just from looking at your drawing?' — this pushes children from representation toward expression. Students who prefer to write more and draw less may do so; the goal is a personal record of togetherness, not a polished artwork.

assessment_items.question_text: In the chapter, Bela's family gathers in the garden in the evenings. Which of the following best describes why the outdoor space matters to the family?

options.label: A
options.text: It is a place where relatives, friends, and neighbours come together to sit, talk, and relax.

options.label: B
options.text: It is used only by the children for playing chhupan-chhupai and peek-a-boo.

options.label: C
options.text: It is a place where the family sells flowers to neighbours.

options.label: D
options.text: It is Dadaji's private space for gardening alone.

assessment_items.annotation: Mark A correct. Distractor B is the most common error — children may focus only on the play element and miss the community dimension. Distractor C has no textbook basis and tests whether students invent details. Distractor D reverses the chapter's portrayal of Bela helping Dadaji in the garden.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe the members and shared activities of a family, connecting a textbook account to their own lived experience.

competency.competency_text: Describes relationships (including between humans and animals/nature) and traditions (art forms, celebrations, festivals) in the family and community

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student attended to the children's games but missed the broader community-gathering function of the garden space described in the section.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has introduced a detail not present in the chapter, suggesting limited engagement with the text.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has confused who works in the garden — the chapter shows Bela helping Dadaji, not Dadaji working there alone.

assessment_items.question_text: Dadiji sings traditional rain songs and has taught them to the children in Bela's family. How does this show that knowledge can pass from one generation to the next? Give one example from the chapter and one from your own life.
expected_elements: Names Dadiji as the source of the rain songs and the children as the receivers of that knowledge.
States that the songs were passed by singing or teaching — an oral method, not from a book.
Provides a personal example of something the student has learned from an older family member, neighbour, or community person.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full credit when all three elements are present. Award partial credit for two elements. The personal example will vary widely — accept any genuine example of learning a skill, song, recipe, game, or practice from an older person. Regional variation in examples is expected and correct.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify and share a folk or traditional song from their own environment, recognising oral transmission as a way knowledge passes between generations.

competency.competency_text: Observes and describes cultural diversity in their immediate environment (food, clothing, games, different seasons, festivals related to harvest and sowing)

expected_elements: Names Dadiji as the source of the rain songs and the children as the receivers of that knowledge.
States that the songs were passed by singing or teaching — an oral method, not from a book.
Provides a personal example of something the student has learned from an older family member, neighbour, or community person.

assessment_items.question_text: The chapter says Dadaji plays traditional games with the children. What does this tell us about how families in the chapter spend time together?

options.label: A
options.text: People of different ages can play and enjoy games together.

options.label: B
options.text: Only grandparents know how to play traditional games.

options.label: C
options.text: Children always teach new games to their grandparents.

options.label: D
options.text: Traditional games are played only during festivals.

assessment_items.annotation: Mark A correct. Distractor B overgeneralises from Dadaji's role and inverts the chapter's message of mutual participation. Distractor C reverses the direction of transmission the chapter shows — elders bring traditional games, children join. Distractor D is a common overgeneralisation not supported by the chapter.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can compare games played across different generations, identifying continuity and change in family and community play traditions.

competency.competency_text: Describes relationships (including between humans and animals/nature) and traditions (art forms, celebrations, festivals) in the family and community

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has read Dadaji's participation as exclusive expertise rather than as shared enjoyment — missing the chapter's intergenerational togetherness message.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has reversed the direction of transmission; the chapter shows elders introducing traditional games, not children teaching elders new ones.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has added a festival condition not present in the chapter, possibly confusing this section with the festival content in 'Helping Each Other'.

assessment_items.task: Munni makes rangoli using colours from dried flowers and leaves she finds around her. Today you made your own rangoli with natural materials. Now draw your rangoli in your notebook and write the name of each material you used. Then write one sentence about where those materials came from.
assessment_items.scaffold: My rangoli used: __________, __________, __________. I found these at __________. My pattern looks like __________.
format_of_output: A drawn or described rangoli design in the notebook
A list of at least two natural materials used
One sentence naming where the materials came from
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any rangoli design — symmetrical or not, simple or complex. The key evidence is the naming of real natural materials (leaves, petals, seeds, bark, soil) and a truthful statement of source (school garden, compound, home garden). Students who made the rangoli on the floor during the activity may draw it from memory. Regional variation in materials is expected and fully correct.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can create a simple design using locally gathered natural materials, connecting the activity to a community craft tradition described in the chapter.

competency.competency_text: Uses local materials to create simple objects (family tree, envelopes, origami animals) on their own for display or use in classroom processes

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can connect a hands-on craft activity to a community tradition described in the chapter, and can record their process through drawing, naming materials, and identifying their source.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold prompts three moves: name materials, name source, describe pattern. A strong response completes all three with specific, truthful details. A weak response names 'things' without identifying them or says 'I don't know' where the source is concerned.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: names two or more specific natural materials by kind (e.g. 'marigold petals, neem leaves'), identifies a real source ('from the school garden'), and describes the pattern in any terms. Weak: names only 'leaves and flowers' without further detail, or omits the source sentence entirely.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who did not participate in the outdoor collection phase may draw a rangoli they have seen at home or in the neighbourhood and name materials they observed being used there. The goal is connection to natural materials and community craft, not a single correct product.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Drawing with labelled list and one written sentence
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: Drawing externalises the student's mental image of their own creation; the list names the natural materials; the sentence anchors the activity to a real source — together these three moves demonstrate the full implied_lo.

assessment_items.question_text: In the chapter, every member of Bela's family contributes to household work — from Dadiji braiding hair to Banku chopping vegetables. Name two household tasks from the chapter and say who does each one. Then name one task you do at home and explain how it helps your family.
expected_elements: Names at least two specific tasks from the chapter (e.g. Dadiji oils and braids Bela's hair; Banku chops vegetables; Bela helps Dadaji in the garden; parents share cooking and cleaning) and correctly links each task to the right person.
Names a task the student personally does at home.
Gives a reason or explanation for how that task helps — not just names it.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full credit for all three elements. Award partial credit when the chapter tasks are correctly named but the personal explanation is absent or vague. The student's own task will vary by household; any genuine household contribution is acceptable. Regional variation in household practices is expected and correct.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe and record how household work is shared among family members, noticing patterns of contribution and care.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: Names at least two specific tasks from the chapter (e.g. Dadiji oils and braids Bela's hair; Banku chops vegetables; Bela helps Dadaji in the garden; parents share cooking and cleaning) and correctly links each task to the right person.
Names a task the student personally does at home.
Gives a reason or explanation for how that task helps — not just names it.

assessment_items.task: Think about a happy moment you have shared with your family — a game, a meal, an outing, a song, or anything else. Draw that moment and write two sentences below your drawing: one sentence saying what is happening, and one sentence saying how you felt.
assessment_items.scaffold: In my drawing: __________. I felt __________ because __________.
format_of_output: A drawing of one happy family moment
One sentence describing what is happening in the drawing
One sentence expressing a feeling and giving a reason
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any genuine family moment — there is no single correct answer. The drawing does not need to be detailed; what matters is that it represents a real shared experience. The two sentences should be the student's own words. Accept regional variation in what 'happy family moment' looks like — a harvest meal, a festival, a daily walk, a game in an alley are all equally valid.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can represent a personal experience of family togetherness through drawing and writing, connecting it to the chapter's themes of shared play and intergenerational care.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can draw on personal lived experience to represent family togetherness, and can articulate both what happened and how it felt — connecting experience to expression.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold has two moves: describe the scene and express a feeling with a reason. A strong response completes both moves with specific detail. A weak response draws something unrelated to family, or writes only 'I felt happy' without any reason.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: the drawing clearly depicts people doing something together; the first sentence names the activity and who is there; the second sentence names a specific feeling and links it to what happened. Weak: drawing is present but the written sentences are missing or say only 'fun' without elaboration.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find drawing difficult may write three sentences instead of drawing. Students who wish to write in their home language for the feeling sentence may do so and add an English word if they can. The goal is personal expression of togetherness, not a fixed product format.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: Drawing allows children to represent scenes and relationships that words alone may not fully capture at this stage; the two sentences build the habit of pairing visual expression with verbal reflection — both are modes this chapter and its competency explicitly value.
